body.statement: Let \(U,R_1,R_2\) be mutually independent real random variables, with \(U\) nonconstant, and let \(r,s\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).  Then the two random variables \(rU+R_1\) and \(sU+R_2\) are not independent.  No moment or centering condition is required.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\phi_U,\phi_1,\phi_2\) for the characteristic functions of \(U,R_1,R_2\).  Suppose, for contradiction, that
\[
Y=rU+R_1
\quad\text{and}\quad
Z=sU+R_2
\]
are independent.  Mutual independence of \(U,R_1,R_2\) gives, for all \(t,v\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{i(tY+vZ)}\right]
=\phi_U(rt+sv)\phi_1(t)\phi_2(v).
\]
Independence of \(Y,Z\) gives for the same quantity
\[
\mathbb E[e^{itY}]\mathbb E[e^{ivZ}]
=\phi_U(rt)\phi_1(t)\phi_U(sv)\phi_2(v).
\]
We next verify directly that the two noise characteristic functions do not vanish near zero.  For \(j\in\{1,2\}\), choose \(K_j\ge1\) such that \(\Pr(|R_j|>K_j)<1/8\).  The elementary inequality \(|e^{iy}-1|\le |y|\), applied on \(\{|R_j|\le K_j\}\), and the bound \(|e^{iy}-1|\le2\), applied on its complement, give
\[
|\phi_j(t)-1|
\le \mathbb E[|e^{itR_j}-1|]
\le |t|K_j+2\Pr(|R_j|>K_j).
\]
Consequently \(|\phi_j(t)-1|<1/2\), and hence \(\phi_j(t)\ne0\), whenever \(|t|<1/(4K_j)\).  Put \(h_j=1/(4K_j)>0\).  Because \(r,s\ne0\),
\[
\rho=\min\{|r|h_1,|s|h_2\}>0.
\]
For \(|p|,|q|<\rho\), substitute \(t=p/r\) and \(v=q/s\) in the preceding identities and cancel the two nonzero noise characteristic functions.  This yields the local multiplicative equation
\[
\phi_U(p+q)=\phi_U(p)\phi_U(q).
\]
Taking \(q=-p\) and using \(\phi_U(-p)=\overline{\phi_U(p)}\), we obtain
\[
|\phi_U(p)|=1\quad (|p|<\rho).
\]

Let \(U'\) be an independent copy of \(U\).  Choose nonzero \(p,q\in(-\rho,\rho)\) with \(p/q\notin\mathbb Q\).  For either \(w\in\{p,q\}\),
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[e^{iw(U-U')}\right]
=\phi_U(w)\phi_U(-w)=1.
\]
The integrand has modulus one, so equality of its real-part expectation to one implies \(e^{iw(U-U')}=1\) almost surely.  Thus, almost surely,
\[
p(U-U')\in2\pi\mathbb Z
\quad\text{and}\quad
q(U-U')\in2\pi\mathbb Z.
\]
The irrationality of \(p/q\) forces \(U-U'=0\) almost surely.  If \(F_U\) is the distribution function of \(U\), independence of \(U,U'\) now implies, for every \(x\in\mathbb R\),
\[
0=\Pr(U\le x<U')=F_U(x)(1-F_U(x)).
\]
Hence \(F_U(x)\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(x\).  The limits and right-continuity of a distribution function then show that \(F_U\) is the distribution function of a point mass, contradicting that \(U\) is nonconstant.  Therefore \(Y\) and \(Z\) cannot be independent.
